title: Faulty Router in Copper-to-Fibre Upgrade Caused FAA Ground Stop, Duffy Says
excerpt: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said a router changed during L3Harris's routine maintenance flooded the air traffic network, and that more than 20,000 flights have been disrupted since Friday.
body:
• Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Saturday that Friday's nationwide FAA ground stop was triggered during contractor L3Harris's routine work switching FAA telecom lines from copper to fibre at a remote location.
  • A replaced router flooded other routers with more than 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, destabilising data at 17 of the FAA's 22 en route centers, officials told Reuters.
  • More than 20,000 flights have been disrupted since Friday, with about 9,000 cancellations on Friday and a further 4,000 to 5,000 on Saturday.
  • Duffy said the FAA expects to be back to full schedule integrity by the end of Sunday, and that there is zero evidence of a cyberattack or anything nefarious.

The nationwide ground stop that halted US air traffic for nearly five hours on Friday was caused by a contractor's routine upgrade work on the Federal Aviation Administration's ageing telecom network, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Saturday — the most specific official account yet of how the longest nationwide ground stop since the September 11, 2001 attacks began.

Duffy told reporters that L3Harris, a longtime FAA contractor, was doing routine maintenance to switch telecommunication lines from copper wire to fibre-optic cable at a remote location when a router change went wrong. The new router began flooding other routers in the air traffic control system with more than 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, causing communications and radar-feed problems, according to Al Jazeera's report of the briefing.

"We had a contractor make a mistake."

— Sean Duffy, US Transportation Secretary

What officials say happened

Officials told Reuters there may have been problems with routers installed in both Arkansas and Texas. The overload hit communications at 17 of the FAA's 22 en route centers, and the agency issued the nationwide ground stop because it could not identify a root cause. The FAA said communications did not go down entirely, but data at the centers became unstable. Duffy said the investigation has not yet settled the central question: "We're working to determine whether we had incompetence, meaning was it user error or installer error from L3Harris, or did they install a faulty router? We haven't determined what the fault was."

L3Harris said in a statement that a system upgrade activity on Friday, November 13 "coincided with the FAA ground stop" and that it is fully supporting the FAA's investigation. The company noted it has completed more than 70% of the planned conversion of airspace communications from legacy copper wires to a fibre-optic system.

The scale of the disruption

The shutdown has disrupted more than 20,000 flights since Friday, Reuters reported. About 9,000 flights were cancelled on Friday and nearly 5,000 more on Saturday, out of roughly 41,000 scheduled Saturday flights. Duffy said the FAA expects to reach "full schedule integrity" by the end of Sunday. Travellers with flights this weekend should still expect residual delays as airlines reset aircraft and crew rotations — and, as our earlier coverage noted, carriers including Air India issued advisories for US routes during the stop (Air India warns of US flight delays after FAA ground stop).

An old network, a known problem

Duffy said the routers being replaced are about 25 years old and were supposed to be replaced in 2006. The FAA spends about $1 billion a year maintaining its old copper-wire system while racing to replace it with fibre-based communications. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said there was no evidence of anything nefarious or AI-related, and that an upgrade of the system is planned by the end of the year. Friday's failure follows a pattern: a 2023 nationwide ground stop, which lasted 90 minutes and disrupted 11,000 flights, was caused by a government contractor unintentionally deleting files, Reuters noted. Our earlier report traced how the initial probe pointed to the overloaded ageing network (Trump rules out cyberattack as FAA ground stop probe points to overloaded aging network); Saturday's briefing identifies the specific work that produced that overload.

What's next

Duffy said the FAA will share its root-cause analysis with airlines once it better understands what failed, and pledged, "We will make sure it never happens again." The open questions for that analysis are whether the fault lay in the router itself or in how it was installed, and whether the same replacement work at other sites carries the same risk before the copper-to-fibre conversion is complete.
